issues.legal_issue: A holder of inalienable jagir property has only a limited interest, and a reversioner may claim a share of compensation when the property is compulsorily acquired.
material_facts: The acquired lands formed part of an inalienable jagir originating in the Cis-Sutlej States.
The holder had not established that the lands had become his absolute property through acquisition by him or his ancestors.
His son claimed the reversionary interest and sought a share of the compensation.
issues.conclusion: The holder was only a limited owner, and the son was entitled to represent the reversionary interest and share in the compensation.
issues.legal_principle: The applicable rules governing the jagir made it inalienable and gave its holder only a limited interest, with the property passing to the successor or reverting to the Government if there was no legal heir. The Court also noted that the same conclusion followed from the Punjab customary law applicable to ancestral immovable property. The Court relied on the historical and administrative materials concerning the jagir and affirmed the concurrent findings below; it did not rely on a cited earlier judicial decision for this conclusion.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_disp: The dispute concerns how compensation for compulsorily acquired property should be distributed.
predicates.acquired_property_was_inalienable_jagir: The acquired property formed part of an inalienable jagir.
predicates.current_holder_had_only_limited_interest: The person holding the property when it was acquired had only a limited interest in it.

issues.definition: When compensation is disputed for property in an inalienable jagir held by a limited owner, the reversioner is entitled to share in the compensation.

issues.legal_issue: The equitable principle governing compensation for property that its owner could not alienate does not justify permanently investing the compensation while allowing the interested persons to receive only its income.
material_facts: The property was held by a limited owner who could not alienate it.
The reversioner sought permanent investment of the compensation so that the holder and the reversioner would receive only its income.

The Court considered the statutory scheme for compensation where an owner lacks power to alienate property and held that temporary investment pending the purchase of substitute land did not support permanent investment.
issues.conclusion: The compensation was not required to be permanently invested; it could be apportioned between the interested persons.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(1)(a) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, provides for compensation to be applied to the purchase of other land held on corresponding terms. Section 32(1)(b) permits investment in securities only as an interim measure when that purchase cannot be made immediately. The Court held that the equitable principle added to the applicable acquisition scheme did not extend to permanent investment. It considered Shri Somashekhar Swami v. Bapusaheb Narayanrao Patil, K. C. Banerjee, Official Receiver, In re, Mt. Gangi v. Santu, and Special Deputy Collector, Ramnad v. Rajah of Ramnad, which had applied the principle in other settings.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_disp: The dispute concerns compensation for property taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquired_property_was_held_by_person_wit: The acquired property was held by a person who lacked power to alienate it.
predicates.permanent_investment_of_compensation_was: An interested person sought to have the compensation permanently invested so that the parties would receive only its income.

issues.definition: When compensation for property held by a person without power to alienate it is disputed, a request for permanent investment does not prevent the compensation from being apportioned.

issues.legal_issue: Equitable apportionment of compensation for property held by a limited owner may account for the risk that the compensation will not reach the reversioners and the need to safeguard the reversionary interest.
material_facts: The holder and his son had competing interests in compensation for three villages forming part of the inalienable jagir.
The son relied on the holder's past conduct and alienations to argue that the share paid to the holder would not reach the reversioners; the Court found those apprehensions difficult to reject.
The son also had a child, and the Court considered the need to safeguard the reversionary interest in the property.
The lower tribunal had apportioned the compensation three-quarters to the holder and one-quarter to the son.
issues.conclusion: The compensation for the three villages was to be divided equally between the holder and the son.
issues.legal_principle: The applicable compensation scheme required equitable apportionment where there was a limited interest or a dispute about entitlement. The Court treated the risk that compensation paid to the limited owner would not reach the reversioners, and the need to safeguard the reversionary interest, as relevant equitable considerations. The equitable apportionment principle had been added to the 1948 acquisition scheme by the 1951 amendment and retained in section 8(3) of the 1953 Act; the Court held that the earlier scheme governed the compensation and its apportionment in this case.

predicates.compensation_apportionment_dispute: The parties dispute how compensation for acquired property should be apportioned.
predicates.acquired_property_was_held_by_limited_ow: The acquired property was held by a person with only a limited interest.
predicates.reversionary_interest_requires_safeguard: The court must account for the need to protect the interest of those entitled to the property after the limited holder.
predicates.compensation_paid_to_current_holder_was_: The evidence supports an apprehension that compensation paid to the current holder would not reach the reversioners.

issues.definition: When compensation for property held by a limited owner must be apportioned, and the reversionary interest needs protection from the risk that the holder will dissipate the compensation, the compensation is divided equally between the holder and the reversioner.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot obtain a distinct share of an increase in compensation on a claim that was not raised before the earlier decision-makers.
material_facts: The son argued that the increase in compensation awarded by the arbitrator should be paid to him alone because his objections had led to the reference and award.
He had not raised that claim before the arbitrator or the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not allow the son to raise the claim for the first time in the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to consider a claim that had not been raised before the arbitrator or the High Court. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_compensation_award: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a compensation award.
predicates.claim_was_not_raised_before_earlier_deci: The party did not present the claim to the decision-makers whose determinations are under appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a compensation award, a claim not presented to the earlier decision-makers is not entertained for the first time on appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A person whose immovable property is compulsorily acquired and possessed is entitled to interest on compensation for the period before the compensation is paid or deposited, unless the governing law clearly excludes that entitlement.
material_facts: The State took possession of the claimants' immovable property before paying or depositing the compensation.
The acquisition statute expressly applied section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, but the Court found that this did not exclude the principles underlying sections 28 and 34 of that Act.
The claimants sought interest from the taking of possession until payment or deposit of compensation.

The Court directed interest at four per cent per annum and allocated it according to the parties' respective compensation interests, including the maintenance beneficiary's entitlement to interest on compensation for the village charged for her maintenance.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest from the date the State took possession until the compensation was paid or deposited; interest on the compensation for the village charged for maintenance was payable to the maintenance beneficiary, and interest on the other compensation was payable equally to the holder and the reversioner.
issues.legal_principle: The taking of possession of immovable property generally implies an obligation to pay interest on its value, because interest takes the place of the owner's right to retain possession. The Court applied Swift & Co. v. Board of Trade, Birch v. Joy, and Inglewood Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd. v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, and approved Surjan Singh v. The East Punjab Government. It held that section 5(e) of the 1948 Act, by applying section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, did not exclude the general rule or the principles underlying sections 28 and 34 of that Act. The proviso to section 1 of the Interest Act, 1839, saved interest otherwise payable by law; the Court referred to Bengal Nagpur Railway Co. Ltd. v. Buttanji Ramji on that proviso. It distinguished the relevant observations in Seth Thawardas Pherumal v. The Union of India in light of Nachiappa Chettiar v. Subramaniam Chettiar.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_of_immovable_prop: The proceeding concerns immovable property taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.state_took_possession_before_compensatio: The acquiring authority took possession before paying or depositing compensation.
predicates.governing_law_did_not_clearly_exclude_in: The governing law did not clearly show an intention to deny interest for the period between possession and payment.

issues.definition: When an acquiring authority takes possession of immovable property before paying compensation, and the governing law does not clearly exclude interest, the claimants are entitled to interest for the resulting period of deprivation.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot challenge on appeal an arrangement that the party's counsel proposed and that the court finds fair and just.
material_facts: The compensation for one village was to be invested, with the annual income paid to the person entitled to maintenance from that village.
The maintenance beneficiary challenged that arrangement on appeal.
Her counsel had suggested that the arrangement be made, and the Court considered it fair and just.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not allow the maintenance beneficiary to challenge the arrangement on appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the fact that the arrangement was fair and just and had been proposed by the challenging party's counsel; it cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_compensation_arrangement: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an arrangement for distributing or managing compensation.
predicates.appellant_or_counsel_proposed_the_same_a: The appellant or the appellant's counsel had proposed the arrangement being challenged.
predicates.arrangement_was_fair_and_just: The court finds the arrangement fair and just.

issues.definition: On appeal, a challenge to an arrangement is rejected when the appellant or counsel proposed that arrangement and the court finds it fair and just.
